scenarios.description: Finding the longest period of consistently increasing stock prices to identify sustained growth trends and optimal holding periods.
Identifying the longest sequence of compatible version upgrades where each version requires features from the previous version.
Analyzing employee or system performance data to find the longest period of continuous improvement or growth.

solutions.title: Recursion
solutions.approach: Use recursive backtracking with two parameters: current index i and previous index j. At each position, choose to either include the current element (if it's greater than the previous) or skip it. Return the maximum length found.
solutions.explanation: The recursive solution explores all possible subsequences by making a binary choice at each position: include or exclude. We track two indices: i (current position) and j (index of the last element included in the subsequence, initially -1). At each position i, we first try excluding nums[i] by calling dfs(i+1, j). If j is -1 (no previous element) or nums[j] < nums[i] (increasing order maintained), we also try including nums[i] by calling dfs(i+1, i) and adding 1 to the length. We return the maximum of both choices. The base case is when i reaches the end of the array, returning 0. This approach explores all 2^n possible subsequences.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution works by exhaustively exploring all possible subsequences. The key insight is that for each element, we have two independent choices: include it in the current subsequence (if it maintains the increasing property) or skip it. The recursive function tracks the index of the last included element (j) to check if the current element (at index i) can be included (nums[j] < nums[i]). By trying both options and taking the maximum, we ensure we find the longest increasing subsequence. The base case handles when we've processed all elements. While correct, this approach has exponential time complexity due to solving the same subproblems repeatedly.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Top-Down) - I
solutions.approach: Add 2D memoization to the recursive solution. Store results for each (i, j) pair where i is the current index and j is the previous index. This eliminates redundant computations by caching results.
solutions.explanation: This solution optimizes the recursive approach by adding memoization. We create a 2D memo array where memo[i][j+1] stores the length of the longest increasing subsequence starting from index i with the previous element at index j (j+1 because j can be -1). Before computing dfs(i, j), we check if we've already solved it. If memo[i][j+1] is not -1, we return the cached result. Otherwise, we compute it using the same logic as the recursive solution and store the result before returning. This transforms the exponential solution into polynomial time by ensuring each (i, j) state is computed exactly once.

solutions.why_it_works: Memoization eliminates the exponential time by caching results for each unique (i, j) state. The key observation is that the longest increasing subsequence starting from index i with previous element at index j depends only on i and j, not on how we reached this state. This creates overlapping subproblems - the same (i, j) pair can be reached through different paths. By storing the result the first time we compute each state, all subsequent lookups are O(1). The memo uses j+1 as the column index to handle j=-1 (mapping it to column 0). This preserves the correctness of the recursive solution while achieving polynomial time complexity.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Top-Down) - II
solutions.approach: Use 1D memoization where memo[i] represents the length of the longest increasing subsequence starting from index i. Instead of tracking the previous element's index, iterate through all possible next elements and recursively find the maximum.
solutions.explanation: This solution uses a different recursive formulation with 1D memoization. Instead of tracking both current and previous indices, dfs(i) computes the longest increasing subsequence starting from index i. For each position i, we initialize LIS to 1 (the element itself), then iterate through all positions j > i. If nums[i] < nums[j], we can extend the subsequence starting at i with the subsequence starting at j, so we update LIS = max(LIS, 1 + dfs(j)). We cache results in memo[i] to avoid recomputation. The final answer is the maximum of dfs(i) for all starting positions i. This formulation is more intuitive and uses less space than the 2D approach.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up) - I
solutions.approach: Convert the 2D top-down solution to bottom-up. Build a 2D DP table where dp[i][j+1] represents the longest increasing subsequence starting from index i with previous element at index j. Iterate backward to fill the table.
solutions.explanation: This solution converts the 2D memoized recursion to iterative bottom-up DP. We create a 2D array dp[n+1][n+1] where dp[i][j+1] stores the LIS starting from index i with the previous element at index j. We iterate i from n-1 to 0 (backward) and j from i-1 to -1 (backward). For each (i,j) pair, we first compute the length without including nums[i] by taking dp[i+1][j+1]. If j==-1 or nums[j]<nums[i], we can include nums[i], so we update with max(current, 1+dp[i+1][i+1]). The answer is dp[0][0] (starting from index 0 with no previous element). This eliminates recursion but uses O(n^2) space.

complexity_explanation.space: The dp table is of size (n+1)×(n+1), requiring O(n^2) space. No recursion stack is needed.

solutions.why_it_works: Bottom-up DP works by building solutions to larger problems from solutions to smaller problems. The recurrence is the same as the top-down solution: dp[i][j+1] depends on dp[i+1][j+1] (exclude nums[i]) and possibly dp[i+1][i+1] (include nums[i]). By iterating backward (from n-1 to 0 for i, and from i-1 to -1 for j), we ensure that when we compute dp[i][j+1], the values dp[i+1][*] have already been computed. The base case is implicit: dp[n][*] = 0 (no elements left). This eliminates recursion overhead but maintains the same O(n^2) space and time complexity as the top-down version.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up) - II
solutions.approach: Use 1D DP array where LIS[i] represents the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at or starting from index i. For each position i, check all positions j after i, and if nums[i] < nums[j], update LIS[i] = max(LIS[i], 1 + LIS[j]). Return the maximum value in the LIS array.
solutions.explanation: This is the most common and intuitive DP solution for LIS. We create a 1D array LIS where LIS[i] stores the length of the longest increasing subsequence starting from index i. We initialize all values to 1 (each element alone is a valid subsequence). We iterate backward from n-1 to 0. For each position i, we check all positions j > i. If nums[i] < nums[j] (can extend the subsequence), we update LIS[i] = max(LIS[i], 1 + LIS[j]). After processing all positions, the answer is the maximum value in the LIS array, as the longest subsequence could start from any position. This solution is O(n^2) time and O(n) space, making it more space-efficient than the 2D approaches.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution defines LIS[i] as the longest increasing subsequence starting from index i. The recurrence relation is: LIS[i] = max(1, max(1 + LIS[j]) for all j > i where nums[i] < nums[j]). By iterating backward, we ensure that when we compute LIS[i], all values LIS[j] for j > i have already been computed. The initialization LIS[i] = 1 handles the base case (each element alone is a valid subsequence). Taking the maximum across all positions gives the answer because the LIS could start from any index. This is the most practical O(n^2) solution, offering a good balance between simplicity, space efficiency, and clarity.

solutions.title: Segment Tree
solutions.approach: Use coordinate compression to map values to indices, then use a Segment Tree to efficiently query the maximum LIS length for all values less than the current value. Update the segment tree with the current value's LIS length. This achieves O(n log n) time complexity.
solutions.explanation: This advanced solution uses a Segment Tree data structure to optimize the LIS computation. First, we compress coordinates by mapping each unique value to a rank (index in sorted order). This allows us to use array indices for the segment tree. For each number in order, we query the segment tree for the maximum LIS length among all smaller values (indices 0 to num-1), add 1 to get the current LIS length, then update the segment tree at the current number's index. The segment tree supports O(log n) range maximum queries and point updates, making the total time complexity O(n log n). While more complex than standard DP, this demonstrates an advanced technique applicable to range query problems.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution optimizes the DP approach by using a segment tree for efficient range queries. The key insight is that LIS[i] = 1 + max(LIS[j] for all j where nums[j] < nums[i]). Instead of iterating through all previous elements (O(n) per element), we use coordinate compression to map values to indices, then use a segment tree to query the maximum LIS among all smaller values in O(log n) time. Coordinate compression is necessary because segment tree indices must be in a bounded range. The segment tree maintains the maximum LIS length for each value range, allowing us to quickly find the best extension for the current element. This transforms the O(n^2) DP into O(n log n) using an advanced data structure.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming + Binary Search
solutions.approach: Maintain an array dp where dp[i] is the smallest tail element for an increasing subsequence of length i+1. For each number, use binary search to find its position in dp. If it's larger than all elements, append it. Otherwise, replace the first element >= it. The length of dp at the end is the LIS length.
solutions.explanation: This is the optimal solution using a clever DP approach with binary search. We maintain an array dp where dp[i] stores the smallest ending element of all increasing subsequences of length i+1. For each number in nums, we use binary search to find the leftmost position where the number should be inserted to maintain sorted order. If the number is larger than all elements in dp (position == len(dp)), we append it, extending the longest subsequence. Otherwise, we replace dp[position] with the number, potentially enabling longer subsequences in the future. The key insight is that replacing with a smaller number doesn't change the current LIS length but may allow longer subsequences later. The length of dp is always the LIS length. Binary search gives O(log n) per element, resulting in O(n log n) total time.

code.code:
from bisect import bisect_left
class Solution:
    def lengthOfLIS(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        dp = []
        dp.append(nums[0])

        LIS = 1
        for i in range(1, len(nums)):
            if dp[-1] < nums[i]:
                dp.append(nums[i])
                LIS += 1
                continue

            idx = bisect_left(dp, nums[i])
            dp[idx] = nums[i]

        return LIS

complexity_explanation.space: The dp array can grow to size n in the worst case (when the entire array is strictly increasing), requiring O(n) space.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution maintains a crucial invariant: dp[i] is the smallest possible tail element for an increasing subsequence of length i+1. This works because we want to keep tails as small as possible to maximize chances of extending subsequences. When we encounter a number larger than all elements in dp, we can extend the longest subsequence. When we encounter a smaller number, we use binary search to find where it fits. Replacing dp[idx] with a smaller number doesn't change the current LIS length but creates potential for longer subsequences later. The binary search finds the leftmost position where nums[i] could be placed, which is the length of the longest subsequence we can extend with nums[i]. The final length of dp equals the LIS length because dp[i] exists only if there's a valid subsequence of length i+1.
common_mistakes: Thinking dp stores the actual LIS - it doesn't, it stores the smallest tails for each length.
Using bisect_right instead of bisect_left, which would allow equal elements in the subsequence.
Not understanding why replacing elements works - it maintains potential for longer subsequences.
Trying to reconstruct the LIS from dp directly - requires additional tracking.
pro_tips: This is the optimal solution for LIS and the preferred approach in interviews.
The dp array is always sorted, which is why binary search works.
Python's bisect_left finds the leftmost position where the element should be inserted to maintain sorted order.
To reconstruct the actual LIS (not just its length), you need to track parent pointers or indices.
This algorithm is also known as Patience Sorting.
